description: Ми — команда студентів із досвідом участі в хакатонах і змаганнях. Наші сильні сторони включають програмування, веб-розробку та дизайн. Нам подобається розв'язувати проблеми, вивчати нові технології та перетворювати ідеї на практичні проєкти. Ми раді принести наші навички та креативність у NASA Space Apps Challenge! 🚀
summary:
Outpost Academy is a free browser game that lets kids aged 7–12 run a Moon or Mars outpost and feel the trade-offs behind real missions. Each day the player shares a few energy blocks between air, a radiation shield, food and water. There is never enough for everything, so every choice gains something and costs something. After each day the game explains what happened, why, and what could have been done differently, so kids learn from mistakes without punishment.

The game uses real NASA data: today's strongest solar flare from DONKI sets how hard the storm is, so the shield decision depends on real space weather. Players can also replay historic storms such as X28 (2003). A card from NASA OSDR shows real astronaut-health research. Every photo is from NASA with credit, and every data card says "Live from NASA" or "From NASA records, not live".

It works on any phone or laptop, with no account and no ads. It has a grown-up mode with discussion questions and 10 languages.
Play: https://sofiazaharchuk.github.io/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer/ | Code: https://github.com/sofiazaharchuk/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer
details:
What it does: Outpost Academy is a free browser game for kids aged 7–12. The player runs a Moon or Mars outpost. Each day they share a few energy blocks between air, a radiation shield, food and water, end the day, and see a report of what happened and why. Every choice gains something and costs something; there are no free options. There are 8 levels (5 on the Moon, 3 on Mars). Each level adds one new idea so young players are not overwhelmed. On Mars, help from Earth arrives the next sol, which models communication delay. Random events make each playthrough different.

Benefits and intended impact: kids experience one real constraint of deep-space survival (resources are always limited and every decision has a cost) and learn from mistakes without punishment. The game is free, works on any phone or laptop with no account and no ads, so it can be used at home and in classrooms. A grown-up mode adds discussion questions. There are 10 languages (English and Ukrainian complete, the rest in beta).

Real data: today's strongest solar flare from NASA DONKI sets how hard the storm is, so the shield decision depends on real space weather. A card from NASA OSDR shows real astronaut-health research (a saved NASA answer, labelled "not live"). Every card says "Live from NASA" or "From NASA records, not live".

Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS. The simulation logic is separate from the interface and covered by automated tests. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/sofiazaharchuk/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer

What is creative: instead of facts or a lecture, the player makes a real trade-off, and after a bad day the game shows a chain of causes ("what happened, because..., so you could have..."). Real NASA space weather links a game decision to real science.

Factors we considered: simple language for ages 7–12; at most 2–3 resources at the start; honesty about data (we never present saved data as live); accessibility (big text, easy-to-read font, less motion, light and dark theme). Honest limits: the numbers are a teaching model, and Mars weather is a scenario inspired by real events.

Source code: https://github.com/sofiazaharchuk/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer

AI use: we used the AI assistant Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, texts and draft translations. The idea, game rules, choice of NASA datasets, fact checking and testing were done by our team. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.
